rules.title: Santa Ana Rent Stabilization Ordinance: annual rent increase cap
rules.requirement:
Annual residential rent increases are limited to the lower of 3% or 80% of the percent change in the CPI over the most recent 12-month period. If the CPI is negative, no increase is permitted.

The City publishes the allowable increase by June 30 each year, effective September 1. The current figure is 2.87% for September 1, 2026 through August 31, 2027.

An owner may petition for relief from the cap by showing that a larger increase is needed for a fair and reasonable return. The City Manager or designee decides within 60 days of a complete application.

Owners must give written notice of the Ordinance and tenant rights at the start of a lease or with any rent-increase notice.

Tenants may petition to contest:
- increases above the cap;
- reduced housing services or habitability failures;
- unauthorized or excessive capital-improvement pass-throughs.

Landlords may, but are not required to, pass through the rental registration fee. The pass-through is charged per rental unit, not per tenant, up to $50. A landlord who charges more must reimburse the overpayment.
rules.key_value: Lower of 3% or 80% of 12-month CPI change; 2.87% for Sept. 1, 2026 - Aug. 31, 2027; no increase if CPI is negative; registration-fee pass-through capped at $50 per unit

coverage.summary: Residential rental buildings constructed on or before February 1, 1995, and mobile home spaces offered for rent on or before January 1, 1990. Buildings constructed after February 1, 1995 and mobile home spaces first offered for rent after January 1, 1990 are exempt.
coverage.construction_date_basis: Construction date; the source says only 'constructed' and does not name the record used
coverage.other_conditions: Mobile home spaces are covered only if offered for rent on or before January 1, 1990. Owners may petition for a fair-return increase above the cap.

rules.exemptions: Residential buildings constructed after February 1, 1995; mobile home spaces offered for rent after January 1, 1990.
rules.effective_date_note: The City Council adopted the ordinance on a Tuesday night in 2021; the exact adoption date is not stated. It took effect November 19, 2021. Each year's allowable increase runs from September 1 to August 31; the current period ends August 31, 2027. That date ends the rate period, not the ordinance.
rules.citation: Santa Ana Rent Stabilization and Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
citation_aliases: Santa Ana Rent Stabilization and Just Cause Ordinance
rules.quoted_span: Increase in residential rents are limited to the lower of 3% per year, or 80% of the percent change in the Consumer Price Index over the most recent 12-month period.
rules.review_note: Neither official document gives a municipal code section or ordinance number, so the citation is by ordinance name; verify against the ordinance text. The construction-date basis is not stated, so year_built is used for 'constructed'. The page does not say whether the $50 registration-fee pass-through is a monthly or annual amount. Precedence: the state cap (Civ. Code § 1947.12) exempts housing under a stricter local rent control, and this cap of at most 3% is stricter. Units outside this ordinance (e.g. built after Feb. 1, 1995) may still fall under the state cap.
rules.source_notes: Both official sources (city press release D085 and city rent stabilization page D084) give the same formula. D084 supplies the 2026-27 figure and the pass-through rule. DX19 mentions the ordinance only in passing. A candidate's sunset date of 2027-08-31 was the end of the current rate period and was removed.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: 2.87 percent is the maximum allowable rent increase for the period of September 1, 2026 through August 31, 2027.
The increase cannot be more than 3% of your current rent or 80% of the Consumer Price Index (CPI) change, whichever is less.
The rent cap does not apply to residential buildings constructed after February 1, 1995, or to mobile home spaces offered for rent after January 1, 1990.
If a landlord charges a tenant a pass-through fee greater than $50, the landlord shall reimburse the tenant for the registration fee pass-through overpayment.
The City was the first in Orange County to approve a rent stabilization ordinance limiting rent increases for certain types of residential properties and creating new protections against eviction.

rules.title: Santa Ana Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
rules.requirement:
After a tenancy has lasted 30 days, an owner may not terminate it without just cause, stated in a written notice.

At-fault causes include default in rent, breach of a material lease term, nuisance and criminal activity. No-fault causes include owner move-in, removal of the property from the rental market, and demolition or substantial remodel.

Before serving an at-fault termination notice, the owner must first give notice of the violation and time for the tenant to fix it.

For a no-fault termination, the owner must either pay 3 months of relocation assistance or waive rent for the final 3 months of the tenancy.

Owners had to notify existing tenants of these protections before December 19, 2021. They must also notify tenants at lease commencement or renewal.
rules.key_value: Just cause required after 30 days of tenancy; notice and opportunity to cure before an at-fault termination; no-fault termination requires 3 months' relocation assistance or waiver of the final 3 months' rent

new_construction_exemption.basis: housing produced in the last 15 years (reference date and measuring record not stated; appears rolling)

coverage.summary: Residential rental property in Santa Ana after 30 days of tenancy. Exempt: housing produced in the last 15 years, deed-restricted affordable housing, hotel and transient occupancy, hospital and care facilities, dormitories, and other shared living quarters.
coverage.construction_date_basis: Housing 'produced' in the last 15 years; basis not stated
coverage.other_conditions: Applies after 30 days of tenancy. The exemption list is introduced with 'including', so it may not be complete.

rules.exemptions: Housing produced in the last 15 years; deed-restricted affordable housing; hotel and transient occupancy; hospital and care facilities; dormitories; other shared living quarters.
rules.effective_date_note: Adopted on a Tuesday night in 2021; the exact adoption date is not stated. Effective November 19, 2021. The notice to existing tenants was due before December 19, 2021.
rules.citation: Santa Ana Rent Stabilization and Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
citation_aliases: Santa Ana Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
Santa Ana Rent Stabilization and Just Cause Ordinance
rules.quoted_span: After 30 days, an owner shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in a written notice.
rules.review_note: Neither official document gives a municipal code section or ordinance number; verify against the ordinance text. The sources are city summaries and give no full list of causes and no notice periods. Precedence: Civ. Code § 1946.2(i) lets a local just-cause ordinance adopted after Sept. 1, 2019 apply instead of state law if it is more protective and contains a binding finding saying so. This ordinance is more protective (30 days vs. 12 months; 3 months' relocation vs. 1 month), but the documents do not show the binding finding. Housing produced in the last 15 years falls back to the state rule, which has its own 15-year certificate-of-occupancy exemption.
rules.source_notes: Official city press release (D085) and city web page (D084). The relocation requirement is folded in because the sources describe it as part of the same ordinance. DX19 mentions the eviction protections only in passing.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: Under a no-fault just cause termination, the owner shall either provide 3 months of relocation assistance or waive payment of rent for the final 3 months of the tenancy.

The Just Cause Ordinance shall not apply to certain types of residential property, including housing produced in the last 15 years; deed-restricted affordable housing; hotel and transient occupancy; hospital and care facilities; dormitories; and other shared living quarters.
Your landlord must have a valid reason to evict you. This could be for not paying rent, breaking the lease, or if the landlord wants to move into the property themselves.

rules.title: Santa Ana ban on algorithmic rent-setting devices (Ord. NS-3090)
rules.requirement:
Prohibits the sale, licensing, provision and use of algorithmic rent-setting software ('Algorithmic Devices') for residential rental property in Santa Ana. Covered tools set rents using nonpublic competitor data, such as real-time rents, lease renewals and occupancy levels.

The ban does not apply to pricing software that relies solely on publicly available data or aggregate historical data, or to tools used to comply with affordable housing program requirements.

An affected tenant may sue for injunctive relief, damages, or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, plus attorney's fees. The tenant need only prove the landlord used the prohibited technology, not intentional collusion. Per a law-firm alert, violations accrue per month.

The City expects to enforce mainly through its existing code enforcement system.
rules.key_value: Ban on sale, licensing, provision and use; tenant civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation (per month per law-firm alert) plus attorney's fees; effective April 2, 2026

coverage.summary: Residential rental property within Santa Ana city limits; no size, age or owner exemptions stated.
coverage.other_conditions: Excludes software relying solely on public or aggregate historical data and affordable-housing compliance tools. Designed to operate alongside state antitrust law.

rules.exemptions: Pricing software that relies solely on publicly available data or aggregate historical data; tools used to comply with affordable housing program requirements.
rules.effective_date_note: First reading was Feb. 17, 2026, and the final vote was set for March 3, 2026 (a Tuesday). The OCBJ article reports that a Tuesday final vote adopted the ordinance. The adoption date is inferred from the scheduled vote; the effective date of April 2, 2026 comes from a law-firm alert and is 30 days after March 3.
citation_aliases: Santa Ana algorithmic rent-setting software ordinance
rules.quoted_span: Ordinance NS-3090 prohibits specified anticompetitive automated rent price-fixing; private tenant claims and up to $1,000 per violation and per month.
rules.review_note: All sources are secondary. No municipal code section, official ordinance text or definition of 'Algorithmic Devices' is captured. Confirm the March 3, 2026 adoption and April 2, 2026 effective date against the ordinance. The state Cartwright Act provision (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729, eff. Jan. 1, 2026) operates alongside this ordinance; the documents raise no preemption question. The Apartment Association of Orange County's criticism is policy argument, not a legal conflict.
rules.source_notes: DX19 (city press release republished by PublicCEO, Feb. 2026) reported only the first reading, so its candidate was marked pending. It describes this same ordinance, which later sources (DX18, DX06) report as adopted and effective, so it is merged rather than kept as a separate pending measure. DX18 says the final vote 'put the ordinance into effect'; DX06 gives the effective date as April 2, 2026, consistent with a 30-day post-adoption effective date. The secondary descriptions of the $1,000 fine/penalty are consistent.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: Santa Ana Ordinance No. NS-3090 (effective April 2, 2026)

The ordinance, approved on Tuesday, Feb. 17, for a first reading and set for a final vote on March 3, prohibits the sale, licensing, provision and use of certain algorithmic rent-setting software for residential rental properties.

The new algorithmic rent-setting ordinance is limited to residential rental property and does not apply to pricing software that relies solely on publicly available data, aggregate historical data, or tools used to comply with affordable housing program requirements.
Under the ordinance, a tenant affected by a violation may seek injunctive relief, damages, or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, plus attorney’s fees.
Landlords caught using the banned software could be fined $1,000. The measure passed its first vote on Feb. 17, and Tuesday’s vote was the final step to officially put the ordinance into effect.
